newsitem.title: USA: U.S. consumer groups attack utility rescue plans.
newsitem.headline: U.S. consumer groups attack utility rescue plans.

text.p: Consumer advocates are up in arms in California, Massachusetts and Pennsylvania, fighting state plans to save utilities from bad past investments as they move into competitive power markets.
At stake are $200 billion in assets, including nuclear power plants, that utilities across the country estimate will be unprofitable in a more competitive market.
Up until now, utilities have been able to recoup the costs of those investments, good or bad, in their rates.

The industry and regulators say that in the shift to open power markets it would be unfair to leave utilities stranded with expensive nuclear plants and power purchase contracts that regulators approved years ago, which in the worst cases could bankrupt some companies.

In California and Pennsylvania, deals have been worked out to allow utilities to pay off those investments -- known as stranded costs -- through bonds and in their rates for several more years. At the same time, the utilities have guaranteed rate freezes or rate cuts during the transition to a fully competitive market.
California is set to open its electricity market to competition on Jan. 1, 1998, and Pennsylvania plans to begin phasing in competition a year later.

Utilities say consumers will be better off with the stranded cost recovery plans because they set a deadline for the utilities to collect their money instead of saddling rate payers with those costs over the life of the assets.

"It is still cheaper for consumers," said Bill Sessa, a spokesman for Pacific Gas and Electric Co., one of California's big three utilities. "The real key to lower electric rates ... is refinancing debt."

But small customers say they should never have had to pay for those bad investments. They do not want to be charged for the investments when they should be seeing their rates drop as they shop for cheaper power supplies.

"They're attempting to force rate payers to back bonds ... so (utilities) can pay off their own mistakes in the form of nuclear power and be at a competitive advantage vis a vis other suppliers who haven't made those mistakes," said consumer advocate Harvey Rosenfield of the coalition Californians against Utility Taxes.
"Give consumers the benefits of deregulation immediately," said Rosenfield, whose group includes consumer, free-market and environmental groups.

The federal government's Energy Information Administration gave consumers ammunition this week in a report that said if states let utilities recoup all stranded costs in the deregulated market, homeowners will see no change in electric rates in the short term instead of the 8-15 percent drop they would see if the utilities did not get their way.

In California -- where $28 billion in assets are at stake -- the coalition is considering a lawsuit challenging the legality of $9 billion in utility bonds approved by the state and designed to cover the costs of a 10 percent rate cut to homeowners and small businesses. The group is also considering a ballot initiative to stop the stranded cost recovery plan.

In Pennsylvania, a similar coalition has already turned to the courts, appealing the state public utility commission's decision to allow PECO Energy Co. to collect $1.1 billion through bonds backed by its customers.

Andrew Altman, deputy director of the Clean Air Council, a state environmental group, said environmentalists had gotten on the bandwagon because they wanted to ensure there was fair competition not only to lower rates but to allow clean energy supplies to enter the marketplace.
Pennsylvania consumers are challenging a state law deregulating the power market, saying it was rushed through the General Assembly without following required procedures.
In Massachusetts, consumer groups are pressuring state lawmakers to rethink stranded cost recovery proposals in legislation this fall.

"I'm now convinced that there's really going to be a debate on this," said Rob Sargent, legislative director for the Massachusetts Public Interest Research Group. "People now take us seriously. Earlier, we were written off as demagogues."
